title: Laplace mechanism
description: The foundational DP mechanism: add noise drawn from the Laplace distribution scaled to the query's sensitivity divided by epsilon. Counting queries get Laplace(1/ε) noise — simple, composable, and the textbook example of turning a privacy definition into an algorithm.
method: Compute sensitivity Δf; sample noise ~ Lap(Δf/ε); release f(D) + noise; each query spends ε from the budget.
usage: Use for numeric queries; compute sensitivity carefully (it's the security-critical number).

demo.code:
import random, math
random.seed(6)
true_count, eps = 1000, 0.5
noise = -math.log(1 - random.random()) / eps * (1 if random.random() < 0.5 else -1)
print(f'true 1000 -> released {true_count + noise:.0f} (Laplace, eps=0.5)')

title: Exponential mechanism
description: For non-numeric outputs (pick the best category, the median), the exponential mechanism samples outputs with probability proportional to exp(ε·score/2Δ). It brings DP to selections and rankings — choosing privately, not just counting privately.
method: Score each candidate; sample with weight exp(ε·score/2Δ); higher scores more likely; the choice is ε-DP.
usage: Use for private selection; bound the score sensitivity carefully.

title: Synthetic data with DP
description: Instead of answering queries, generate a synthetic dataset with DP guarantees (via DP-GANs, MST, or marginal-based methods) and let analysts query it freely. The synthetic data preserves statistical patterns while no synthetic row corresponds to a real person — privacy once, utility many times.
method: Learn DP-noisy marginals or train a DP generative model; sample synthetic rows; validate utility on target workloads.
usage: Validate synthetic data on your actual workloads; regenerate when workloads change.

demo.code:
print('synthetic: 10k rows, DP eps=1.0')
print('workload queries: within 3% of real-data answers')

title: Private query answering (PINQ)
description: PINQ-style frameworks wrap LINQ-like queries with automatic sensitivity analysis and noise: analysts write normal queries, the framework computes sensitivity from the query structure and adds the right noise. Privacy by construction for data analysts, not just privacy engineers.
method: Write queries in the framework; it derives sensitivity; adds calibrated noise; deducts from budget automatically.
usage: Route analyst queries through the framework; never let raw queries touch sensitive tables.

demo.code:
print('query: count(users where age > 30)')
print('framework: sensitivity 1, eps 0.1 -> noisy count 4,812 (true 4,800)')

title: Composition theorems
description: Running k ε-DP queries gives kε-DP (basic composition); advanced composition and RDP give tighter bounds — the math that makes multi-query analysis affordable. Composition is why the budget accountant can be precise instead of paranoid.
method: Apply basic/advanced/RDP composition to bound total loss; use the tightest applicable theorem; the accountant implements them.
usage: Use RDP accounting in practice; understand which theorem your accountant implements.

demo.code:
print('100 queries, eps=0.1 each: basic -> 10.0; RDP -> 2.3')
print('tighter composition: 4x more queries for the same budget')

title: Privacy-utility tradeoff curves
description: Every ε buys utility and spends privacy; the tradeoff curve plots accuracy vs ε so stakeholders choose deliberately. Publishing the curve — 'at ε=1 we get 92% accuracy, at ε=0.1 we get 78%' — turns the privacy parameter from magic number into business decision.
method: Sweep ε; measure utility; plot the curve; choose ε with stakeholders; document the choice.
usage: Always show the curve; never pick ε by default; revisit as data grows.

demo.code:
curve = [(0.1, 0.78), (0.5, 0.88), (1.0, 0.92), (2.0, 0.94)]
print('eps -> accuracy:', curve)
print('chosen: eps=1.0 (92%) — documented with stakeholders')

title: Local differential privacy
description: In local DP, noise is added on the user's device before data ever leaves — the server never sees raw data. Apple's and Google's telemetry use it: the aggregator learns population statistics while each individual's contribution is deniable. Trust nobody with raw data.
method: Randomize responses client-side (randomized response); aggregate noisy reports; the server only ever sees noise.
usage: Use when users don't trust the collector; expect higher noise (local DP costs more utility).

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(9)
true = 1
reported = true if random.random() < 0.75 else 1 - true  # randomized response
print(f'true {true} -> reported {reported} (plausible deniability)')

title: DP-SGD for private training
description: DP-SGD trains neural networks with differential privacy: clip per-example gradients (bounding sensitivity), add Gaussian noise, and account privacy via the moments accountant. It's how industry trains on sensitive data — the model learns patterns without memorizing individuals.
method: Clip gradients to norm C; add Gaussian noise; update; track (ε,δ) with the moments accountant; stop at budget.
usage: Tune the clipping norm (too small biases, too large wastes budget); track ε throughout training.

demo.code:
print('epoch 10: eps spent 2.1 / 8.0, accuracy 91% (non-private: 94%)')
print('privacy cost of 3 accuracy points: quantified')
